Isoperimetric

GeometryCurvesCircles
Game: Drag the hollow dots to reshape the red curve, then see whether the smaller blue copies are longer, shorter, or the same length.
How to play: Choose Arcs, Lines or Free hand. Drag a dot (or focus it and use the arrow keys); the buttons change how many dots there are and flip the copies.
Look for the math

The applet shows three families of curves between the same two points. In each one the red curve is single and the blue curves are copies that fit into the gaps along the same baseline. The question on the original page is simply: in each family, which is longer?

The claim on the page

The page calls the shapes isoperimetric: the red and blue boundaries have equal length. Its explanation gives the semicircle case and says of the other two families that an independent proof from two sets of parallel lines is obvious. The logic test below checks all three, not just the first.

Semicircles

A circle of diameter D has circumference P = πD, so a semicircle has arc length ½πD. If the small semicircles have diameters D1, D2, ... that abut along the big diameter, then D1 + D2 + ... = D and

½πD1 + ½πD2 + ... = ½π(D1 + D2 + ...) = ½πD

So the lengths are equal no matter where the break points sit. That is the exact claim in the explanation: a semicircle and a row of abutting semicircles on its diameter are isoperimetric. The X-alternate checkbox turns every other small arc upside down without changing its length.

Broken lines

Here the red curve is A → M → B. Over a gap [p,q] of width Δx, drawing through p a parallel to AM and through q a parallel to BM makes a little broken line that is a scaled similar copy of the big one, with scale Δx / AB. Adding all the gaps gives AB again, hence the same total perimeter. X-alternate mirrors every other little V below the line; a mirror changes its position, not its length.

Freehand curves

The red curve is a cubic spline through 21 points. Each blue copy is the same curve under a uniform similarity: both coordinates are scaled by AB / Δx and placed inside its gap. Length scales by that same factor, so the pieces again add up to exactly the red length. Y-alternate turns every other copy over, which also keeps its length.

What the test confirms

The check script transcribes the applet's own PointMover.Reset, arc parameters, GetParallelTo / Intersect construction and CubicSpline.Value a second time, then compares them for every break-point count from 1 to 15 over hundreds of shapes. All three families keep the red and blue lengths equal, confirming the page's claim. Two small interface choices differ from the old applet: a break-point drag is clamped between its neighbours instead of snapping when it gets too close, and the freehand handles move vertically only (as the applet's VPoint does). Neither changes the curve being drawn.

Try Free hand, turn on Y-alternate, and drag the lowest middle dot: the blue copies fold and stretch, yet their total length still matches the red curve.
